## Principle

Distillation is one of the most widely used separation techniques in the process industries, and it is fundamentally based on the differences in volatility between the components of a liquid mixture. When a liquid mixture is heated and partially vapourised, the vapour that is produced is richer in the more volatile component than the liquid from which it was generated, because the more volatile component has a greater tendency to escape into the vapour phase. However, it is important to understand that a single stage of boiling and condensation can only enrich the product to a limited extent, and it cannot deliver a pure product on its own. 

Inside the column, these repetitions take place through intimate contact between vapour rising up the column and liquid flowing back down it. As the vapour leaving a given stage encounters liquid returning from the stage above, an exchange of components takes place between the two phases: the more volatile component transfers into the vapour, while the less volatile component transfers into the liquid. The extent of separation achieved on each stage is governed by the relative volatility, which provides a convenient measure of the relative escaping tendencies of the two components under identical conditions. When the relative volatility is close to unity, each stage delivers very little enrichment and a large number of stages will be needed, whereas when it is well above unity, only a relatively small number of stages may be required.

It is also essential to appreciate the role played by reflux in making the enrichment process cumulative rather than merely repetitive. A portion of the condensed product is returned to the top of the column as liquid reflux, and this returning liquid progressively washes the rising vapour as it passes from stage to stage. Heat is supplied at the base of the column in order to boil the liquid and generate the upward flow of vapour, while heat is removed at the top in order to condense the vapour and provide the reflux. The net result is that the feed is separated into a distillate product that is rich in the more volatile component and a bottoms product that is rich in the less volatile component, with energy being consumed in order to bring this about.

## Equipment

The column itself takes the form of a vertical shell which is fitted with contacting devices distributed along its height. Trays are widely used for this purpose, holding up a layer of liquid through which the vapour is made to pass, with each tray effectively acting as a single contacting stage. Several tray designs are in common use: sieve trays are essentially perforated plates, valve trays incorporate movable caps which adjust the vapour opening in response to the flow, and bubble-cap trays force the vapour to pass up through risers which are covered by caps submerged in the liquid layer. 

The feed is introduced into the column at an intermediate height, at the stage whose composition most closely matches that of the feed itself. Above the feed point, the column serves to enrich the vapour towards the composition of the distillate, while below the feed point it serves to strip the more volatile component out of the descending liquid towards the composition of the bottoms. A reboiler located at the base of the column supplies the heat required for vaporisation, and a condenser located at the top liquefies the overhead vapour. A part of the resulting condensate is withdrawn as distillate product, while the remainder is returned to the column as reflux by way of a reflux drum. 

## Worked example

Let us consider, by way of illustration, a binary feed of composition $z$, where $z$ denotes the mole fraction of the more volatile component in the feed. The objective is for the column to deliver a distillate of composition $x_D$ together with a bottoms product of composition $x_B$, both compositions being expressed as mole fractions of the same component. An overall material balance establishes the relationship between the three flow rates concerned, since the feed rate must equal the sum of the distillate rate and the bottoms rate. A component balance provides a second, complementary relationship, in that the more volatile component entering with the feed must leave divided between the two product streams, in proportion to their respective flow rates and compositions. Taken together, these two balances fully determine the way in which the feed is split between distillate and bottoms once the two product compositions have been specified, and they demonstrate that the split is by no means a free choice: if a purer distillate is demanded at a fixed bottoms composition, a smaller proportion of the feed will report to the overhead product.

Within the column itself, a stepping construction can be used to count the number of stages required. The construction proceeds between the operating relation, which is imposed by the material balances on the liquid and vapour compositions between successive stages, and the equilibrium relation, which determines the vapour composition that can be produced by a liquid of any given composition. Stepping off between these two relations, from the distillate composition down to the bottoms composition, gives one equilibrium stage for each step taken. Where the two relations come close to one another, the steps become progressively smaller and the number of stages required grows without limit, so that the construction also reveals the point at which a specified separation ceases to be attainable at a given reflux. 

The result obtained can be checked by reference to the limiting case. As the relative volatility approaches unity, the equilibrium relation approaches the line of equal compositions, the steps become smaller and smaller, and the number of stages needed to achieve the specified products increases beyond anything that could be contemplated in a practical column. Conversely, as the relative volatility increases, the steps become wider and the separation can be accomplished with only a small number of stages. The example therefore illustrates something that the balances on their own cannot show, namely that purity has to be purchased with stages and with reflux, and that the price of both is ultimately set by the relative volatility of the particular pair of components being separated.

## Limits

It should be borne in mind that the simple model described above treats the relative volatility as though it were constant throughout the column. In a real mixture, however, the relative volatility varies with both composition and temperature, and it may approach unity at some particular composition even where it is comfortably different from unity elsewhere. Where the relative volatility actually reaches unity, the mixture is said to form an azeotrope, and no column operating at that pressure can carry the separation beyond the azeotropic composition, irrespective of the number of stages fitted or the amount of reflux employed.

The notion of the equilibrium stage is itself an idealisation. The streams leaving a real tray are not truly in equilibrium with each other, since the contact time available and the degree of mixing achieved are both finite, with the consequence that a real tray delivers only a fraction of the enrichment that an ideal stage would deliver, and the column requires more trays than the stepping construction predicts. 

Finally, practical operation imposes its own set of limits. If the vapour rises too rapidly it will entrain liquid and flood the column, while if it rises too slowly the liquid will weep through the trays and the quality of contact will be destroyed. The working range of the column lies between flooding and weeping, and the model has nothing to say about this range. In a similar way, the model says nothing about cost: it counts stages and reflux requirements, but the energy cost associated with both of these is left to be evaluated by a separate calculation.

## Principle

Distillation separates a liquid mixture by the difference in volatility of its components. When a liquid mixture is boiled, the vapour formed is richer in the more volatile component than the liquid from which it came, because the more volatile component escapes into the vapour more readily. A single boiling and condensation therefore enriches the volatile component but does not purify it. Distillation repeats the operation many times inside one apparatus, so that each repetition adds enrichment and the product can approach either component in a high state of purity.

The repetitions take place between vapour rising through the column and liquid flowing down. Vapour leaving a stage meets liquid returning from the stage above, and the two streams exchange components: the volatile component passes into the vapour, and the less volatile component passes into the liquid. A stage on which the leaving streams are in equilibrium sets the limit of what one contact can do, and the design counts stages in these equilibrium units. The separation that a stage achieves depends on the relative volatility, which compares the escaping tendency of the two components under the same conditions. Where the relative volatility stands close to unity, each stage enriches the vapour very little and the column needs many stages; where it stands well above unity, few stages suffice.

Reflux makes the enrichment cumulative. Part of the condensed product is returned to the top of the column as liquid, and this returning liquid washes the rising vapour stage by stage. Heat supplied at the base boils the liquid and drives the vapour upward; heat removed at the top condenses the vapour and provides the reflux. The column therefore separates the feed into a distillate rich in the volatile component and a bottoms product rich in the less volatile component, and it spends energy to do so.

## Equipment

The column is a vertical shell fitted with contacting devices along its height. Trays hold a layer of liquid through which the vapour passes, and each tray acts as one contacting stage. Sieve trays are perforated plates; valve trays carry movable caps that adjust the vapour opening to the flow; bubble-cap trays force the vapour through risers covered by caps submerged in the liquid. Packed columns replace trays with a bed of packing that spreads the liquid into films and gives a large area of contact in a continuous manner rather than in discrete stages.

The feed enters at an intermediate height, at the stage whose composition best matches the feed. Above the feed point the column enriches the vapour toward the distillate composition; below it the column strips the volatile component out of the descending liquid toward the bottoms composition. A reboiler at the base supplies the heat of vaporisation, and a condenser at the top liquefies the overhead vapour. Part of the condensate leaves as distillate and part returns as reflux from a reflux drum. Instruments measure temperatures along the column, and the temperature profile indicates where the composition changes most steeply.

## Worked example

Take a binary feed of composition $z$, where $z$ denotes the mole fraction of the volatile component in the feed. The column is to deliver a distillate of composition $x_D$ and a bottoms product of composition $x_B$, with both compositions stated as mole fractions of the same component. An overall balance fixes the relation among the three flow rates: the feed rate equals the sum of the distillate and bottoms rates. A component balance adds the second relation: the volatile component entering with the feed leaves divided between the two products, in proportion to their flow rates and compositions. The two balances together determine the split of the feed between distillate and bottoms once the two product compositions are specified, and they show that the split is not a free choice: demanding a purer distillate at a fixed bottoms composition sends a smaller share of the feed overhead.

Inside the column, the stepping construction counts the stages. Between the operating relation, which the balances impose on the liquid and vapour compositions between stages, and the equilibrium relation, which fixes the vapour composition that a liquid of given composition can produce, the construction steps from the distillate composition down to the bottoms composition. Each step is one equilibrium stage. Where the two relations approach each other, the steps become small and the stage count grows without limit; the construction therefore also shows where a specified separation stops being attainable at a given reflux. Raising the reflux moves the operating relation away from the equilibrium relation and reduces the stage count, at the price of vapourising and condensing more material for the same product rates.

The check on the result is the limiting case. As the relative volatility approaches unity, the equilibrium relation approaches the line of equal compositions, the steps shrink, and the stage count required for the specified products rises beyond any practical column. As the relative volatility grows, the steps widen and few stages accomplish the separation. The example therefore shows what the balances alone cannot: purity is bought with stages and with reflux, and the price of both is set by the relative volatility of the pair being separated.

## Limits

The simple model treats the relative volatility as constant along the column. In a real mixture the relative volatility changes with composition and with temperature, and it can approach unity at some composition even where it is comfortable elsewhere. Where the relative volatility reaches unity the mixture forms an azeotrope, and no column operating at that pressure can carry the separation past the azeotropic composition, whatever its stage count or reflux.

The equilibrium stage is also an idealisation. Streams leaving a real tray are not in equilibrium, because contact time and mixing are finite, so a real tray achieves only a fraction of the enrichment of an ideal stage and the column needs more trays than the stepping construction counts. The model further assumes that the molar flows of liquid and vapour stay constant along each section, which holds only where the components have similar heats of vaporisation and the heat losses are small.

Operation sets the remaining limits. Vapour rising too fast entrains liquid and floods the column; vapour rising too slowly lets liquid weep through the trays and destroys the contact. Between flooding and weeping stands the working range of the column, and the model says nothing about it. The model likewise prices nothing: it counts stages and reflux but leaves the energy cost of both to a separate calculation.
